# On the Strange Gift of Boredom

I've been thinking about boredom lately—how we treat it like a disease to be cured rather than a signal worth listening to.

Everyone's optimizing now. Every commute is a podcast, every waiting room a chance to scroll, every quiet moment an inefficiency to eliminate. We've made idleness feel vaguely shameful, like we're wasting the precious resource of our own attention.

But boredom might be where the good stuff happens.

When you're bored, your mind stops performing for an audience (even if that audience is just yourself checking your productivity). It wanders. It makes weird connections. You remember things you thought you'd forgotten. Sometimes you realize something matters to you more than you've admitted.

I notice my best ideas come after sustained boredom—in the shower, on a walk without my phone, lying in bed unable to sleep. Not during the boredom itself, but in the permission it gives my brain to stop striving.

There's also something oddly democratic about boredom. You can't buy your way out of it with enough money or status. The richest person still feels it. Maybe that's why we hate it so much—it reminds us we're not actually that in control.

I'm not saying we should all sit in empty rooms. But maybe boredom isn't a problem to solve. Maybe it's a message: slow down, your brain needs this, something wants your attention but it's too quiet to hear over the noise.

The cure might not be more stimulation. It might be patience.
